title: Two rezonings for apartment towers near transit
subtitle: Victoria Street South mid-rise, King Street West high-rise, affordable units, traffic, construction impacts and heritage interface concerns.
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee held a public meeting on two zoning by-law amendments for rental apartment buildings in transit station areas. It recommended both to Council. Because the committee only recommends, Council must still adopt or change these decisions.

The first covers 169-183 Victoria Street South, where an eight-storey, 28.8 metre building is proposed. The committee recommended approval {{vote:m1}}, along with endorsing the urban design brief. The second covers 864-876 King Street West, next to the Grand River Hospital LRT stop, and the committee recommended approval {{vote:m2}}. Both by-laws under the newer Growing Together zoning will have no force until that by-law is in full effect.

For residents, the decisions add rental housing, including units set aside as affordable under federal financing programs. They also raised questions about traffic, construction impacts, three-bedroom units and how closely new buildings should follow the recently adopted zoning rules.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving amendments to both Zoning By-law 85-1 and 2019-051 to allow an eight-storey, 28.8 metre apartment building.
The committee recommended endorsing the October 2024 urban design brief for Victoria Street South and directing staff to implement it through site plan approval.
The committee recommended that the Victoria Street South amendment to By-law 2019-051 have no force until the Growing Together by-law is in full force and effect.
The committee recommended approving the amendment to Zoning By-law 85-1 for King Pine Kitchener Inc. to enable a high-rise rental development.
The committee recommended approving the matching amendment to Zoning By-law 2019-051, which would take effect only once the Growing Together by-law is in full force.

debate: On Victoria Street South, committee members asked about traffic at the busy Park and Victoria intersection and whether the access on Park Street could be moved. Staff said the traffic study considered nearby planned developments and was found satisfactory by the City and Region, and that two-way Park Street was preferable to one-way Henry Street, where loading would occur.

Several members questioned amending the Growing Together zoning, which is under appeal, so soon after adoption. Staff said the changes are site-specific and minor, meet the intent of the rules, and should not be treated as precedent, though one councillor noted that risk could not be fully removed.

Concerns were raised about a tall building next to the Victoria Park Heritage Conservation District. Staff said they balanced provincial intensification direction with heritage interests and found the interface appropriate.

Members pressed both applicants on three-bedroom units. The Victoria Street applicant committed to three to five such units at site plan, and the King Street applicant said they would be explored at site plan.

A resident delegate on the King Street West item opposed it, citing construction truck traffic on Herbert Street, the amount of green space funding, and shadowing from height. Staff said parkland money goes into a city-wide fund, Herbert Street is slated for reconstruction, and the site has room for construction staging.
